statements.text: Artificial intelligence is a promising technology with the potential to revolutionize a range of industries, but with that promise also comes potential peril, especially to the creators of art and other copyrightable works. [...] It is critical that we think through the many ways that AI will change our lives and whether our existing laws are up to the challenge.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet hearing on AI and copyright law.

statements.text: For creators, for the Copyright Office, and for this Committee, the rise of artificial intelligence, or AI, might pose the greatest challenge yet. AI models, trained on copyrighted data, pose serious intellectual property questions regarding licensing and credit for final products.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Judiciary Subcommittee oversight hearing on the U.S. Copyright Office, focusing on AI and copyright.

statements.text: Many AI models are trained on copyrighted data, but not all the training data is licensed. Why is it important that copyrighted information used to train AI be licensed?
statements.context: Verbatim transcript of a House Oversight Committee hearing on the U.S. Copyright Office.

statements.text: Register Perlmutter, in its guidance, the Copyright Office argued that both the Constitution and the Copyright Act define an author as ``a human entity,'' excluding nonhuman creations, and noted that this stance is reinforced by various court rulings, and concluded that those using AI in their creations can claim copyright protection only for their human contributions. [...] How did the Copyright Office make that determination, and how will that bright line help artists and creators survive in fields that will increasingly be filled with AI-generated works?
statements.context: House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on the U.S. Copyright Office, with a member questioning the Register of Copyrights about AI and copyright policy.

statements.text: China has used AI-generated images to sow discord related to the Maui wildfires a couple of months ago that took 100 American lives. What is America's exposure to deepfakes and AI-generated images from China? How can that hurt us from a security standpoint?
statements.context: House Judiciary IP subcommittee hearing on strategic competition with China, focused on IP theft, cybersecurity, and AI.

statements.text: If the PRC chooses to use AI to increase its authoritarian hold over its own people, to advance its cyber espionage strategy, or to interfere in its neighbor's elections, such actions will undermine competition and innovation, not just in China, but around the world.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on IP and strategic competition with China, focusing on IP theft, cybersecurity, and AI.

statements.text: Dr. Hannas, what role do you think government should play in making sure that deepfakes and AI-generated images do not do us harm either national security or economically?
statements.context: Question posed during a House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on IP and strategic competition with China, focused on IP theft, cybersecurity, and AI.

statements.text: Dr. Hannas, earlier this summer, the cybersecurity—excuse me, the Cyberspace Administration of China released guidelines for the adoption of generative AI technology, which included new requirements for how algorithms are built and deployed, as well as for what information AI developers must disclose to the government and the public. What is the significance of those regulations?
statements.context: House Judiciary IP subcommittee hearing on strategic competition with China, questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: We are here to examine how current laws and future legislation can protect creators from misuse of a technology that is posed to transform the world as we know it. [...] Our question today is not if, but how, Congress should act to protect artists from such treatment.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Judiciary Subcommittee field hearing in Los Angeles on AI and intellectual property.

statements.text: You know, any technology can be used for evil. [...] I think that what you’re going to see right now that various states are trying to step into the space and see how they might be able to control or regulate some of it. You’ve got the private sector, of course, is trying to self-correct and they need to.
statements.venue: Interview with The Hill on AI, deepfakes and election interference

statements.text: Our biggest competitor is China in the space, and they are advancing exponentially with this. So, if we, if Congress, stumbles into this, or overregulates the technology, it could have very serious implications for us with regard national security.
statements.venue: Interview with The Hill on AI, deepfakes and election interference

statements.text: We're watching very closely to see how the private sector adapts to that and how the states regulate or control that. [...] Congress doesn't need to jump out ahead of that and take unnecessary steps, but we'll see how all these ideas percolate.
statements.venue: Axios interview on deepfakes and AI policy

statements.text: we have to be careful not to have 50 different states hyper-regulating AI because it has national security implications. If some of the deep blue states smother it with regulation, as they’re prone to do, then it might hamper our development and it could put us in a compromised position against our enemies: China and others. I think there’s a federal response that’s appropriate here.
statements.venue: Remarks to reporters on the state AI regulation moratorium in the reconciliation bill

statements.text: America will win the AI race. We will win it if two things happen, if government resists the siren song of control and if industry steps up as our patriotic partner. I think we can do both of those things today.
statements.venue: Keynote at 5th Annual Hill and Valley Forum

statements.text: As the Speaker of the House and ultimately somebody who's going to help spearhead this effort in Congress, this is our commitment in a simple summary: simplify and streamline where we can, to regulate only where we must and pave the way for American dominance. In a nutshell, that's our objective.
statements.venue: Keynote at 5th Annual Hill and Valley Forum

statements.text: The first thing is, we have to deliver a single national framework that protects children, safeguards communities, supports creators, and avoids a patchwork of state regulations. We recognize that constant shifts in policy don't just confuse the market, they run contrary to our national interest.
statements.venue: Hill and Valley Forum remarks, as reported by Fox News

statements.text: AI companies have a serious responsibility to earn the trust of the communities they invest in and to be good neighbors. The Ratepayer Protection Act guarantees hardworking American families won’t foot the bill for the buildout of AI infrastructure– or see their energy costs rise to pay for it. Winning the AI race against China means winning here at home, but it can’t come at families’ expense, and this legislation strikes the right balance of protecting local communities while keeping America on the cutting edge of AI development.
statements.venue: Speaker Johnson press release on House passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act

statements.text: If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American. So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.
statements.venue: CNN State of the Union interview with Jake Tapper, as reported by The Hill

statements.text: But we don’t need everybody to panic right now. We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past, and make sure we’re doing everything we can, responsibly, to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously.
statements.venue: CNN State of the Union interview, as reported by The Hill

statements.text: there is an obvious corporate responsibility that the people who are creating these models have to ensure that their products are safe. [...] We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge. It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.
statements.venue: CNN State of the Union interview, as reported by Politico

statements.text: They need to come together in a meeting with us and sit down and figure out what the right balance is. We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us. That’s the challenge. It’s national security, balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.
statements.venue: CNN State of the Union interview, as reported by TheWrap

statements.text: We’re not going to rush in and pass a piece of legislation that would do harm to the country and put China at an edge. [...] And so we’ve got to do this carefully.
statements.venue: NBC Meet the Press interview, as reported by The New York Times

statements.text: They can self-regulate. They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should. [...] We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, Ok? Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.
statements.venue: Remarks to reporters, as reported by New Orleans CityBusiness

statements.text: We do not need a moratorium. We do not need to jump in and hyper regulate this because we'll lose the race to China. The innovation is important to continue.
statements.venue: Fox Business interview, as reported by Newsweek

statements.text: Your rates won’t go up. We want the water resources that they can cycle that inside. There’s a lot of precautions that can be made. And where it’s done well, they partner with the local community. It's a win-win-win, because it provides a lot of jobs, new investment, and that’s what these local communities need.
statements.venue: Fox Business interview on data centers, as reported by The Center Square

statements.text: I hope it's voluntary. [...] We'll find out what comes out of the meeting today. I think that that's where they're headed. I think they see the handwriting on the wall, and I think they want to ensure investors, you know, consumers, the American public, that they're going to do this in a very safe way, and and that will, I think, put us in the right place.
Safety and innovation are not mutually exclusive pursuits. Everyone around the table nodded in agreement and said it in their own words in their own way, but we can do both of these things.
statements.venue: Speaker Johnson remarks to press after meeting with President Trump and superintelligence industry leaders

statements.text: The White House and Congress will continue to guide the industry's development in a safe manner because we owe that to the American people and we will do it. Congress is going to keep steady hands at the wheel on this and will continue to assess and further deliberate in the days ahead.
statements.venue: Speaker Johnson remarks to press after meeting with President Trump and superintelligence industry leaders

statements.text: “AI has begun to demonstrate its potential to improve Americans’ lives. To ensure we continue to harness its potential and beat China in the global AI race, Congress must take action. Today, the Trump Administration took a critical step in releasing a framework that gives Congress a roadmap to pursue legislation that provides innovators with much-needed certainty, while protecting consumers and prioritizing kids’ online safety. House Republicans look forward to working across the aisle to enact a national framework that unleashes the full potential of AI, cements the U.S. as the global leader, and provides important protections for American families.”
